title: Why Time Disappears As You Get Older
description:
A year at age five is twenty percent of your entire life. A year at fifty is two percent. But that is only half the answer. Here is what actually happens to your perception of time.

Made with AI assistance.

#psychology #time #brain #science #facts

scenes.narration: When you were five, a single year was twenty percent of your entire existence. Summer lasted forever. Now a year vanishes before you finish describing it, and most people assume they are remembering childhood badly. They are not. The difference is real, and it is built into how the brain stores time.

The obvious answer is proportion. A year at fifty is just two percent of your life, so of course it feels smaller. The idea is old, it is repeated constantly, and it is genuine. It is also only a small part of the explanation, because the same twelve months can feel fast or slow depending on what you did inside them. Anyone who has survived a dull year and a vivid one already knows the proportion cannot be doing all the work.

There is a simple test that shows proportion is not enough. Ask two people how the last year felt in the moment and you will get two very different answers, fast or slow, depending on whether the year contained a move, a job change, or a long stretch of the same desk and the same route.

The second half is novelty. Your brain does not record time evenly. It records change. New experiences get written down in detail, and repeats get compressed into almost nothing, so the archive you later judge a period by is thin exactly where the days were identical. A year of identical Tuesdays is a single file, not fifty two.

Think about the last trip you took. The first day feels long because almost everything was new. The ride home feels like it took minutes, because your brain skipped it, and there is almost nothing left in the memory to measure it against. Same journey, same distance, opposite lengths.

The pattern has a name people use casually, the holiday paradox. A fortnight feels endless while you are inside it and then looks like a weekend once you are home. Both impressions come from the same brain, and both are honest readings of two different records.

This is why childhood was so dense. Everything was a first. Your first bicycle, your first snow, your first argument, your first bus ride alone. Your brain had a reason to keep all of it, and the reason was that none of it could be predicted.

In laboratory work, single novel items are consistently judged as lasting longer than repeated ones, even when both are shown for exactly the same length of time. The effect is small, reliable and awkward to argue away, because the stimulus does not change. Only the observer's history changes.

Time judgements come in two varieties, and confusing them causes most of the confusion here. Prospective timing happens while you are watching the clock, and it stretches when nothing else is happening. Retrospective timing happens later, out of the memory of the event, and it stretches when the event was full.

Waiting rooms are the laboratory for the first kind. With no stimulus and attention pointed at the clock, minutes behave badly, and most people recognise this version of slow time from the ten minutes before a medical appointment or a delayed flight. Nothing about the room changed. Only what you were doing with your attention.

The second kind is the one that shapes a life. When you later estimate how long a year was, you are not reading a clock. You are sampling the archive, and a year with many distinct entries simply reads as longer than a year with few. Ask anyone to list what happened last year, and the length of the list is the length of the year.

That is what routine does. The commute you have made four hundred times, the Tuesday you have now lived fifty times, none of it is being written in any detail, because the brain does not file a prediction that came true exactly as predicted. The archive needs surprise, and routine is what surprise looks like when it stops happening.

The blur on the way home is the same mechanism operating on a smaller scale. The outbound journey was new, so it is stored as a sequence of scenes. The return is a repeat, so it collapses into a summary, and the summary takes a second to recall.

Absorption does something similar in the other direction. When attention is fully engaged by a task, the clock is not being monitored at all, and hours can pass that leave almost no shape behind them. This is why an evening on the couch can feel both short and empty. The time was spent. It simply was not written down.

Games and feeds are built to keep attention off time and on content, which makes them unusually good at compressing an evening. The session feels brief in the moment and leaves almost nothing in the archive, which is a rarer combination than it sounds. A book from the same evening usually leaves a great deal more behind.

Emotion thickens the archive as well. A crowded summer festival, a wedding, an argument in a kitchen, all of them are stored with far more detail than an average afternoon, and each therefore occupies more space in the retrospective length of that month. This is why difficult years are remembered as long years.

This is why two people can remember the same year differently. One of them was in the same kitchen most evenings, and the other was not, and each is reading their own record rather than misremembering a shared one. Neither account is inaccurate. They are summaries of two different amounts of filing.

Moving house is the standard example. The weeks around a move are remembered as long and eventful, because a move supplies dozens of firsts in a short space of time, from a new route to work to the location of the light switches. The calendar did not change. The number of new entries did.

Learning produces the same effect. The first hours behind the wheel, the first weeks of an instrument, all of them are stored at high resolution, because the brain is still predicting badly and therefore still updating. Competence is compression. The better the prediction gets, the less of it gets written down.

Which is the uncomfortable implication. Expertise is efficient and it is also invisible to the clock. The better you get at something, the less of it you record, and the faster that portion of your life appears to have gone when you look back. Proficiency and forgetting arrive by the same door.

Recent work suggests the acceleration lives mostly in memory rather than in the moment. When people judge duration while an experience is actually happening, age differences come out much smaller than the later recollections suggest, which points at the archive rather than at the clock. The feeling of acceleration is real. Where it lives is the question.

Some of the internal clock is genuinely biological. Timing research describes a pacemaker whose rate moves with arousal and with certain neurochemistry, and states that raise that rate make equal intervals feel longer. It is a real effect, and it operates on seconds and minutes rather than on decades.

Emotion tests that system too. Under threat, people consistently judge the moment as longer than identical neutral moments, and the live debate is about whether the clock sped up or whether the frightening episode was simply stored with unusual density. Either way, frightening minutes are remembered as long ones.

School shows the pattern in miniature. The first term of a school year is remembered as long, the remaining terms shorten, and by June the calendar is moving visibly faster than it was in September, for exactly the reason you would now expect. Nothing changed in the timetable. The number of new Tuesdays fell.

One small trick people use is variety on purpose. Changing the route, the lunch, the order of the evening, or the room where the work gets done supplies just enough novelty that the day registers as a distinct entry instead of a repeat of yesterday.

This is not a suggestion to fill every hour. Dense weeks are not happier weeks, and much of what makes a life good is repetitive by nature. The useful distinction is between repetition chosen for a purpose and repetition that happens because nothing was decided. One is structure. The other is drift.

Travel is the most reliable producer of expanded time, and it does not need to be distant travel. A town you have never visited, an unfamiliar train line, a museum you keep meaning to see, all of them add entries to the archive. The entry does not have to be dramatic. It has to be new.

The strongest counterargument is that every generation has complained that the years go faster, which is true, and which is exactly what a memory based explanation predicts. Each age sees its own archive thinning, and each reads that thinning as the world speeding up. The complaint is consistent. The mechanism is consistent with it.

Another counterargument is that people simply look further back as they age, so any ten year period now contains a smaller fraction of the total. That is also true, and it works alongside the thinning of the archive rather than instead of it. Two modest effects, added together, explain most of the impression.

So the practical reading is narrow and honest. The clock in your head runs at roughly the same speed at thirty five as it did at twenty five. What changed is what you were giving it to file, and how little of the filing you have noticed.

Time does not speed up on its own. You stopped giving it anything worth remembering, and memory is the only yardstick a year is ever measured against. Do something unfamiliar this week, and the week will be longer when you look back at it than the one before it.

Nothing exotic is required. One new street, one conversation outside your usual circle, one recipe you have never made. The archive only needs to notice that something happened, and it is remarkably generous about what counts as something. Novelty is cheap, and it is the only currency this system accepts.

The reason childhood summers felt endless was never that they were longer. They were the same three months, and almost all of it was being written down. A summer with no archive is a week, and a summer with a full one can still be found in detail forty years later.
